subChunks.title: Designing Code Review Culture, Standards & Automation
subChunks.hookHtml: Code review is one of the highest-leverage activities in a software team — it catches bugs, spreads knowledge, enforces standards, and shapes the codebase culture. But most teams treat it as a checkbox. A Lead's job is to design a code review system that is fast, educational, and scalable — not a bottleneck where good PRs go to die.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Purpose of Code Review

Code review serves multiple purposes simultaneously, and conflating them creates problems:

  • Correctness: catching bugs, logic errors, missing edge cases
  • Standards: ensuring code follows agreed patterns and is maintainable by others
  • Knowledge sharing: the reviewer learns the change; the author learns the reviewer's perspective
  • Mentoring: a senior reviewing junior code has a teaching opportunity — questions that explain, not just correct
  • Architecture alignment: ensuring individual changes don't undermine the larger design

When code review primarily serves gatekeeping ('nothing ships without my approval'), it becomes a bottleneck. When it primarily serves learning, quality improves and throughput increases.

Review Standards and Checklists

A code review checklist makes implicit standards explicit and consistent. Good checklist items are specific and actionable — not 'is this good code?' but 'does this method have a unit test for the happy path and at least one error case?' A well-designed checklist reduces cognitive load on the reviewer and removes the 'I didn't know that was a standard' conversation after a PR lands.

Common checklist categories: correctness (logic, edge cases, null safety), tests (coverage, test quality, test isolation), security (input validation, auth checks, sensitive data handling), observability (logging, metrics, errors surfaced), documentation (public API docs, complex logic explained), performance (obvious hot paths, N+1 queries).

PR Size and Author Discipline

The quality of a review is inversely related to the size of the PR. A 50-line PR gets a thorough review in 15 minutes. A 500-line PR gets a glance and an LGTM. Lead responsibility: establish a PR size norm (50–150 lines is a reasonable target for reviewable changes) and coach authors who consistently ship giant PRs.

Techniques for keeping PRs small: feature flags to merge incomplete work safely, splitting infrastructure changes from behaviour changes, working in smaller increments. A PR that changes the interface and the implementation and the tests and the documentation in one batch is reviewable but harder than four smaller PRs.

The Review Comment Taxonomy

Not all review comments are equal. Tagging comments helps authors prioritise:

  • Blocker: must be addressed before merge (correctness issue, security hole)
  • Suggestion: should be addressed but the author can use their judgement
  • Nit: minor style or naming — take or leave, doesn't block merge
  • Question: I don't understand this — not a criticism, a request for explanation
  • Learning: I noticed this pattern and wanted to share — no action required

Without tags, authors treat every comment as a potential blocker and review round-trips multiply unnecessarily.

Automation as a Force Multiplier

Every review comment that can be automated should be automated. Linting, formatting, import order, static analysis, test coverage thresholds, dependency vulnerability scans — all of these belong in CI, not in human review. When a human reviewer spends comments on formatting, they are doing a computer's job and failing to do a human's job. Automate ruthlessly so that human review focuses on: correctness, design, knowledge transfer.

Review Turnaround Time

Review turnaround is as important as review quality. A PR that sits unreviewed for 48 hours causes context switching, delayed deployments, and frustration. A healthy norm: reviews acknowledged within 2–4 hours of business hours; completed within 24 hours for normal PRs. Leads set this norm by modelling it and by treating review turnaround as a team health metric alongside deployment frequency and cycle time.

storyBeats.text: The team's code review cycle averaged 3.5 days. Not because the team was slow — because every PR started a negotiation. Reviewers would catch formatting issues, argument over naming, request tests for things already covered, and leave 'have you considered?' comments with no clear action. Authors didn't know which comments were blockers and which were suggestions. Round-trips multiplied. The Lead introduced three changes: a linter in CI (formatting/style automated out), a comment taxonomy (blockers, suggestions, nits, questions), and a 24-hour review norm. Cycle time dropped to 14 hours within a month.

storyBeats.speaker: Staff Engineer Bram
storyBeats.text: The single most impactful thing I have done for review velocity is to put every automated concern into CI and tell reviewers explicitly: if CI passes, do not comment on it. No formatting comments. No import order comments. No style-guide comments that the linter would have caught. Human review is for things that require human judgement. When reviewers spend their limited attention on things that computers should catch, they have less attention for the bugs that matter.

storyBeats.speaker: Staff Engineer Bram
storyBeats.text: The comment taxonomy changed our culture more than any other intervention. Before: every comment felt like a potential blocker. Authors were anxious; reviewers had to be careful not to seem pedantic. After: 'nit: rename this variable' takes the emotional charge out of a small style preference. 'Blocker: this method doesn't validate the input before calling the external API, which will surface errors as 500s instead of 400s' — that is clearly serious. The taxonomy teaches authors how to triage and reviewers how to communicate intent.

storyBeats.speaker: Staff Engineer Bram
storyBeats.text: PR size discipline is an author skill that you have to explicitly teach and then enforce culturally. A 700-line PR is not reviewed — it is rubber-stamped. The author thinks they are moving fast by batching changes; they are actually producing lower-quality code because nobody has capacity to think carefully about 700 lines. Small PRs with clear descriptions are a form of respect for your reviewer's attention. The Lead models this and names it when they see large PRs: 'can we split this?'

learningObjectives: Explain the multiple purposes of code review and describe how each should influence review behaviour
Design a code review checklist for a Java engineering team with at least five actionable categories
Apply the review comment taxonomy (blocker/suggestion/nit/question/learning) to clarify review communication
Identify which review concerns belong in automation vs human review and explain why
commonMistakes: Using human review for concerns that CI automation could catch (formatting, style, linting) — wastes reviewer attention
Sending every review comment with the same implicit urgency — causes authors to treat nits as blockers and delay merges
Accepting large PRs without pushing back on size — 500-line PRs get rubber-stamped, not reviewed
Setting no turnaround time expectation — PRs sit in review for days, blocking deployment and causing context switching
assessmentCriteria: Can write a PR review checklist for a Java service that has at least 5 specific, actionable categories (not vague like 'is it good code?')
Can take a set of review comments and classify each as blocker/suggestion/nit/question/learning, explaining the classification
Can identify 3 things in a described review workflow that belong in CI automation rather than human review
Can explain the relationship between PR size and review quality, and describe how to enforce a PR size norm
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain code review to an engineer who just joined the team and has only experienced review as 'someone approves before you merge.' What makes a review valuable beyond just catching bugs? What is the comment taxonomy and why does it matter? How does automation change what reviewers should focus on?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
The Academy's engineering team has the following code review problems. For each, identify the root cause and propose a specific fix:

  1. PRs often sit for 3–5 days without a review. Engineers are frustrated with delays but also feel overwhelmed when they open a PR and see 20+ comments.
  2. A Senior engineer leaves detailed comments on every PR — formatting, naming, architecture, correctness, and philosophical observations about design patterns. Junior engineers find reviews demoralising. Senior feels their feedback isn't respected when things are merged without addressing all comments.
  3. The team has a '2 approvals required' rule but half the team typically rubber-stamps large PRs to avoid blocking each other. Security issues have shipped through reviews that technically passed.
  4. After every significant incident, someone identifies that the root cause code had been reviewed and merged. Reviews seem to be missing real correctness issues while catching trivial style issues.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. 3–5 day review cycle + 20+ comment overwhelm:
   Root cause: no review SLA expectation, and reviews are too wide in scope (no taxonomy, no size norm).
   Fixes:
   - Establish a team norm: reviews acknowledged within 4 business hours, completed within 24 hours for normal PRs (> 24 hours only for architectural changes > 300 lines)
   - Introduce comment taxonomy: all comments tagged as Blocker / Suggestion / Nit / Question. Authors merge after all Blockers resolved; Suggestions and Nits at author discretion.
   - Introduce PR size norm: PRs should be under 150 lines of production code change. Reviewers can flag large PRs before reviewing and request a split.
   - The 24-hour norm should be modelled by the Lead — they review first, setting a pace.

2. Senior's comments demoralising juniors:
   Root cause: mixing concerns of different severity/importance without taxonomy; unclear which comments are required. Senior's intent is mentorship but delivery is overwhelming.
   Fixes:
   - Introduce the comment taxonomy — Senior tags each comment. Juniors now know that nit: or suggestion: are optional. This immediately reduces cognitive load.
   - Coach the Senior on 'learning:' comments as a separate category — architectural observations become teaching moments, not corrections.
   - Set an expectation that reviews should be scopeable: if the PR is 60 lines, 20 comments is probably too many unless it has serious correctness issues.
   - Have the Senior do one pairing session with a junior on review approach — show, not just tell.

3. Rubber-stamping + security issues:
   Root cause: '2 approvals' rule without specificity; large PRs overwhelming reviewers; no automation catching obvious security patterns.
   Fixes:
   - Enforce PR size norm — large PRs should be split. Nobody can review 500 lines with care.
   - Add SAST (static analysis security testing) to CI — catches known vulnerability patterns automatically. Human review then focuses on logic-level security issues the tool can't catch.
   - Consider a security checklist item as a required explicit sign-off on PRs touching auth/input validation/data access: reviewer must explicitly comment 'security: reviewed input validation — satisfied' or 'security: this PR doesn't touch auth paths.'
   - Culture change: it is OK to say 'I cannot review this thoroughly — it needs to be smaller' and request a split before starting a review.

4. Reviews catching style but missing correctness:
   Root cause: reviewer attention captured by easy-to-spot surface issues; no structured checklist forcing correctness checks.
   Fixes:
   - Automate everything that automation can catch: linting, formatting, imports, style, basic static analysis. Remove style comments from human review completely — if it is automatable, it is not a review comment.
   - Introduce a correctness-focused checklist: does every non-trivial method have an error path test? Does input validation happen before any side-effects? Are there null safety concerns? Are there race conditions in concurrent code?
   - Add a post-incident review step: for each incident, trace the root cause back through the PR that introduced it and ask 'what would have caught this in review?' Use the answer to improve the checklist.
   - Review quality metrics: instead of counting approvals, occasionally sample reviews to see how often Blockers are being identified correctly.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Design a code review system for the Academy's engineering team (12 engineers, 3 product teams, mixed seniority from Junior to Lead). The team ships approximately 40 PRs per week across 8 services. Current state: no formal review standards, inconsistent review quality, 48-hour average review cycle time, significant variation in what individual reviewers focus on.

Define: (1) A PR size standard with a rationale and enforcement mechanism, (2) A comment taxonomy with definitions and examples, (3) A review checklist for Java Spring Boot services (at least 6 categories, each with 2–3 specific items), (4) What belongs in CI automation vs human review (give 5 examples of each), (5) A review SLA expectation and how you would track and enforce it, (6) How you would improve review culture without making it feel like policing.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
1. PR Size Standard:
   Standard: production code changes should be ≤200 lines (excluding tests and generated code). Encouraged target: ≤100 lines.
   Rationale: studies consistently show review thoroughness decreases sharply above 200 lines; throughput improves with smaller PRs despite more of them.
   Enforcement: GitHub Actions check that warns (not blocks) on PRs > 200 production lines, linking to the splitting guide. CI comment: 'This PR is 380 lines of production code. Consider splitting infrastructure changes from behaviour changes. See: [splitting guide link].' Tech Lead approves exceptions for migrations or unavoidable batch changes.

2. Comment Taxonomy:
   🔴 Blocker: must be resolved before merge. Correctness bug, security issue, missing critical test, violation of non-negotiable standard.
   Example: 'Blocker: getUserSpells() calls the DB without checking that userId matches the authenticated user — IDOR vulnerability.'
   🟡 Suggestion: should be addressed; author can use their judgement. Better design, edge case handling.
   Example: 'Suggestion: this could use Optional.map() instead of the null check, which makes the intent clearer.'
   ⚪ Nit: minor style or naming. Take or leave — does not block merge.
   Example: 'Nit: spellCastedAt → spellCastAt (past tense should be cast, not casted).'
   🔵 Question: I don't understand this — seeking explanation, not requesting change.
   Example: 'Question: why does this method return a list rather than a stream? Is there a caller that needs multiple passes?'
   📚 Learning: sharing context or a pattern — no action required.
   Example: 'Learning: Java 21 records would let you replace this DTO with a one-liner — worth knowing for future.'

3. Review Checklist for Java Spring Boot:

   Correctness:
   - Does every conditional branch have test coverage (happy path + at least one failure path)?
   - Are all external inputs validated before use (null checks, range checks, format validation)?
   - Are there any potential NullPointerExceptions in the new code paths?

   Tests:
   - Are unit tests isolated (no real DB, no real HTTP calls — use Mockito/TestContainers appropriately)?
   - Do test names describe the behaviour being tested, not the implementation ('should return 404 when spell not found' not 'testGetSpell')?
   - Does the test actually assert the right thing, or is it asserting that no exception was thrown?

   Security:
   - Does any endpoint that accesses user data verify that the authenticated user owns the data being accessed?
   - Are secrets/credentials loaded from environment/Secret Manager — never hardcoded?
   - Is any user-controlled input concatenated into SQL, HTML, or shell commands without sanitisation?

   Observability:
   - Are errors logged at the right level (ERROR for unexpected, WARN for expected degraded paths, INFO for important events)?
   - Is the correlation ID (MDC) propagated if new threads are spawned?
   - Are meaningful events logged (spell cast, user created) at INFO or above for audit trail?

   Performance:
   - Is there any potential N+1 query (fetching in a loop)?
   - Is there any obviously expensive operation in a hot path (regex compile, I/O in loop)?

   Documentation:
   - Do public API methods have JavaDoc describing their contract (not implementation)?
   - Is any complex business logic commented with 'why' not 'what'?

4. CI Automation vs Human Review:

   Belongs in CI (5 examples):
   - Code formatting (Checkstyle, google-java-format) — zero-judgement, fully automatable
   - Import ordering and unused imports (IDE/PMD check)
   - Test coverage threshold (JaCoCo ≥80% line coverage required to pass)
   - SAST scan (SpotBugs, Semgrep security rules — known vulnerability patterns)
   - Dependency vulnerability scan (OWASP dependency-check for known CVEs)

   Belongs in human review (5 examples):
   - Whether the design makes the right trade-offs for the problem being solved
   - Whether the test is actually testing the right behaviour (not just coverage)
   - Whether the error handling is appropriate for the business context (log and continue vs fail fast)
   - Whether a new abstraction is justified or adds unnecessary complexity
   - Whether the change will be understood by the next engineer who reads it in 18 months

5. Review SLA:
   Expectation: PRs acknowledged within 4 business hours of opening; full review completed within 24 business hours. PRs > 200 lines: 48-hour SLA.
   Tracking: GitHub Actions webhook → Slack notification for PRs unreviewed after 4 hours during business hours ('⏰ [PR name] has been open for 4 hours with no reviewer — link'). Weekly Lead review of median and p90 review cycle time from GitHub Insights or LinearB.
   Enforcement: the Lead models the SLA by reviewing first and acknowledging PRs promptly. Teams discuss SLA breaches in retrospective as a process problem, not a blame event.

6. Improving culture without policing:
   - Make the standards explicit and visible (checklist, taxonomy posted in the team handbook) — removes 'I didn't know' friction
   - Pair on reviews early: new engineers shadow an experienced reviewer for 2–3 PRs before reviewing solo
   - Rotate review assignments to avoid the same reviewer always catching the same things
   - Monthly '5-minute review highlight' in team meeting: share one review that was particularly good (caught a real bug, excellent teaching comment, productive discussion) — celebrates review quality without scorekeeping
   - Never use review statistics punitively ('you only approved 3 PRs this week') — trust erodes and rubber-stamping increases
   - Post-incident: trace PRs that introduced incidents, add learnings to the checklist — reviews become part of quality improvement, not bureaucracy

questions.questionHtml: What is the primary purpose of a code review comment taxonomy (blocker/suggestion/nit/question)?
options: To clarify the priority and required action for each comment, reducing ambiguity and unnecessary round-trips
To rate the overall quality of a PR
To document which reviewers are most thorough
questions.correctAnswer: To clarify the priority and required action for each comment, reducing ambiguity and unnecessary round-trips
questions.explanationHtml: Without a taxonomy, authors treat every review comment as a potential blocker, creating anxiety and multiple unnecessary round-trips. A taxonomy makes intent explicit: a 'blocker' must be resolved; a 'nit' is optional preference that doesn't block merge; a 'suggestion' invites author judgement. This reduces the cognitive and emotional overhead of reviews, speeds up cycle time, and preserves the important distinction between genuine correctness issues and style preferences.

questions.questionHtml: A reviewer leaves a comment on a PR: 'You should use Optional here instead of returning null.' This is true but not a correctness issue — the current code works safely. How should this comment be tagged?
options: Blocker — null returns are always wrong in Java
Nit — it is a minor style preference with no impact
Suggestion — it is a legitimate improvement but not required to merge
Question — the reviewer doesn't understand the design
questions.correctAnswer: Suggestion — it is a legitimate improvement but not required to merge
questions.explanationHtml: Using Optional instead of null return is a meaningful code quality improvement — it makes the possibility of absence explicit and prevents callers from ignoring it. But if the current code handles null safely and there is no correctness issue, it is not a blocker. Tagging it as Suggestion signals: 'I think this is better and you should consider it, but I trust your judgement and won't hold the merge.' Blocking a working PR for Optional style is a disproportionate response; ignoring the concern entirely loses the learning opportunity.

questions.questionHtml: Human code reviewers should leave comments on formatting, import ordering, and code style issues that are caught by linters and CI tools.
questions.explanationHtml: If a concern can be caught and enforced automatically by CI (linters, formatters, static analysis tools), human reviewers should not spend their limited attention on it. Every comment a human writes about formatting is a comment they didn't write about correctness, design, or knowledge transfer — which are the things only humans can assess. The principle: automate everything automatable, reserve human review for human judgement. When reviewers repeatedly comment on things that CI could catch, it signals that the automation setup is incomplete, not that review thoroughness is high.
